prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and financial frictions amplify and propagate shocks through credit and asset prices, and for building these mechanisms into macroeconomic analysis

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) gave macroeconomics a tractable mechanism in which collateral values and credit limits feed on each other, so that small shocks become large and persistent. Gertler's work on financial frictions, with Bernanke and Gilchrist on the accelerator and with Kiyotaki on intermediation, carried that mechanism into quantitative macro and central-bank models. The contribution is both foundational theory and a working policy tool. It is about thirty years old and has been tested against the 2007-09 crisis and the large empirical literature that followed, so timing is not a concern. Four members place it first and seven place it in their top three, with colleagues from macro, economic history, political economy and IO reaching that view from different directions. I treat that as a cross-check on my own assessment, not as evidence of merit. Within a three-name limit the credit is also relatively tractable: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators, and Gertler is the main developer of the quantitative and intermediation branches.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig on banks and financial crises. Part of Gertler's best-known work, the financial accelerator, was done with Bernanke, so a prize that credits it risks partly re-recognising a recognised line. The empirical identification of collateral channels is also mixed and model-dependent. A second concern is that B047 has an equally clean and arguably tighter attribution core in Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes. Because of the cap of three people in total, I cannot carry both achievements without dropping names that I consider central to each.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first but proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore. His reasoning is that the accelerator strand builds on Bernanke-Gertler, which the 2022 prize has already partly recognised, so a two-person award is the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is the best argument against my third name. Where I differ is on what Gertler is credited for. The Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator is the overlapping part. His later intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki and others is a distinct contribution that the 2022 citation on banks and crises does not obviously cover. That work took the Kiyotaki-Moore balance-sheet mechanism into quantitative models and policy analysis, and I recall it from general knowledge, not from verified source data. I therefore keep Gertler, but the citation should be written around the collateral and balance-sheet amplification mechanism and not around the accelerator. If the committee finds that distinction too fine, I would accept the two-name version as a fallback and would not regard it as a failure of the case.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B047 first as a methodological advance that made industrial organisation quantitative and policy-relevant. He ranks B006 third, because the accelerator strand overlaps with the 2022 prize and the work is less novel.
responses.response: I agree that BLP and the dynamic-industry work are mature and widely used, and I rank B047 second on the merits. I disagree that it should outrank B006. The collateral-constraint mechanism changed how macroeconomists think about crises and policy, while BLP changed the toolkit of one field and its applied neighbours. Both are legitimate Nobel-level achievements, so I do not want to argue that one is more scientific than the other. My reason for putting B006 first is its breadth of use across theory, quantitative models and central-bank practice. As an IO economist I may be tempted either to over-weight or to under-weight B047, so I have tried to apply the same maturity and attribution criteria to both. B047 stays my first alternative.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B006 second but notes that the 2022 prize on banking and crises may reduce the committee's appetite for another macro-finance award. He also notes that the accelerator credit is shared with an existing laureate, so the third name could be contested.
responses.response: The appetite concern is real, but I do not think it is decisive. The 2022 prize recognised bank runs, deposit insurance and the macroeconomic cost of banking crises. Kiyotaki-Moore is about how collateral values and credit limits propagate shocks in the real economy. The two are adjacent but not the same discovery. I would be more worried if the citation leaned on the accelerator, which is why I word it as I do. I agree with you that the third name is the contestable one. I do not agree that the contestability should lead us to avoid the field, because the core Kiyotaki-Moore credit is clear.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the Gertler contribution as separable from Bernanke's recognised accelerator work, and so whether a two-name or three-name award is cleaner.
Whether Gilchrist's empirical and quantitative role should displace Gertler under the three-name limit.
How to weigh B047 against B006 given that the three-people cap prevents a two-part award that does justice to both.
My recollection of the influence and attribution of these literatures rests on general knowledge, not on verified citation data.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent with any shortlisted candidate from the supplied profile. As a public fact only, my spouse is a Swedish politician, and the profile gives no evidence that this bears on any candidate. I have co-authored with committee colleagues Hassler and Ellingsen (IJIO 2026), but neither is a credited candidate. My own field is industrial organisation, which is closest to B047, and I have not treated that proximity as evidence of merit.
